title: The Last Stroke Flicks Out
youtube_title: Her real signature flicks out at the end. These two don't.
logline: Nora tapes copies of the property agreement and the rights transfer to a light box and checks them against her old drafts. She can see they're traced. A judge needs an expert to say it.
hook: The light box glows from below. Two photocopies side by side. She leans over her own name: "My last stroke flicks out. Like pulling a glass rod."
mid_hook: She spreads every pre-marriage sketch across the floor. Every signature flicks at the end. The two on the light box pause at every turn. "Traced."
extra_hooks: Sparks, loud: "So it's fake!" Dana doesn't look up. "You can see it. A judge can't."
conflict: The ferry terminal entry is in; results take two weeks. First she has to prove those two signatures aren't hers, and her own eye doesn't count. A court-appointed examiner has to see it.
turn: She thinks the two signatures matching perfectly is their mistake. Dana says that's exactly the tell: nobody signs the same way twice. Only a tracing matches.

cliffhanger.text: Dana lays a motion on the light box. "We ask the court for an examiner. He'll make you sign in front of him. One shaky signature, we lose." Nora picks up the pen. It hovers over the blank page.
cliffhanger.question: Can she sign her own name?

spectacle: Light from below shines through both photocopies; the two signatures overlap, and every pause in the ink glows as a small black dot.
glamour_shot: She bends over the light box, lit from below, her shoulder-length hair brushing the glass, eyes tracing the signature stroke by stroke.
general_payoffs: She sees that both signatures pause at every stroke: traced
Dana drafts a motion asking the court to appoint a document examiner
locations: Remelt Studio (light box, sketches on the floor)

title: Her Samples Don't Count
youtube_title: Expert granted. His lawyer says her old drafts don't count
logline: The court appoints a document examiner. Then Leonard Fisk's brief calls her pre-marriage drafts "of unknown origin." Overnight, the only samples she has stop counting.
hook: The court's order arrives at Remelt: motion granted, examiner Arthur Wexler. She clips it to the light box beside the two photocopies.
mid_hook: Fisk's opposition follows: "The plaintiff's own drafts are of unknown origin. Likely made after the fact." Dana slaps it down. "He wants you unable to prove you're you."
extra_hooks: Peg reads the brief through her reading glasses and snorts. "Grant did that with homework. Wrote the date first."
conflict: The examiner needs her everyday signature to compare. All she has are drafts she carried out herself, and one line from Fisk turns them into her word against his.
turn: She thinks the fight is about signatures. Fisk is fighting about who gets believed: if she supplied the samples, the defense can say she practiced.

cliffhanger.text: Last line of the order: the examiner will collect live samples at the plaintiff's studio in three days; counsel for both sides may attend. Dana looks up. "Fisk will come. He'll watch you sign."
cliffhanger.question: Will her hand shake for Fisk?

spectacle: The court order and the two photocopies hang side by side on the light box; the light turns all three pages nearly transparent, the text on their backs bleeding through in reverse.
glamour_shot: She reads the order at the light box, apron still on, sleeves rolled, the light catching her jaw from below, lips pressed tight.
general_payoffs: The court grants the motion and appoints examiner Arthur Wexler
She reads Fisk's play: make her samples her word against his

title: Ten Signatures
youtube_title: Ten signatures as his lawyer watched. One reply shut him up
logline: Arthur Wexler watches Nora sign ten times at Remelt. Fisk says she'll add the flick on purpose. Wexler says what he really needs is a signature she never had in her hands.
hook: Ten blank sheets on Remelt's long table. Wexler pulls on black sleeve covers. "Ten times. Normal speed." Across the table, Fisk twirls his fountain pen.
mid_hook: On the seventh, Fisk speaks up. "She knows to flick. Of course she flicks." Wexler keeps his ruler on the page. "She can add a flick. She can't fake speed."
extra_hooks: After the tenth, her hand is steady. Wexler holds one sheet up to the light box, then looks at her for the first time.
conflict: She has to sign ten natural signatures with her ex-husband's lawyer watching: no shaking, nothing forced. Fisk is waiting for the smallest difference.
turn: Ten signatures should settle it. Wexler says they only show how she signs today. To prove the two are traced, he needs signatures from before the marriage, held by someone else.

cliffhanger.text: Wexler folds his ruler. "One thing's missing. Before the marriage. Dated. Held by someone else." He looks at her. "Do you have one?"
cliffhanger.question: Who holds her old signature?

spectacle: Ten sheets in two rows on the long table, the same name ten times, every last stroke flicking out, the light box glowing at the table's edge.
glamour_shot: She signs, wrist turning, the last stroke flicking out; the faint burn scars inside her wrist move with it, and she doesn't stop when her hair falls forward.
general_payoffs: She signs ten times in front of Fisk without a single shake
Wexler shuts down the "fake flick" claim: she can add a flick, not speed

title: A Second Plate
youtube_title: At 1 a.m. she made pasta and left a second bowl at his door
logline: Sleepless while she waits on the report, Nora cooks pasta in the Ashford kitchen and makes a second plate. At the study he keeps closed, her hand stops in the air.
hook: 1 a.m. One light on in the Ashford kitchen. She plates the pasta, looks at the pot, and fills a second bowl.
mid_hook: She carries it to the study. House rule three: the study is off-limits. Her knuckles stop an inch from the door. She doesn't knock.
extra_hooks: In the living room Peg is still knitting under the lamp, something very small. She stuffs it under a cushion. "What are you looking at? Bed."
conflict: She's waiting on a report that decides everything. She owes this house a door and a dinner table, and she has no idea how to say thank you to a closed study.
turn: She thinks she just can't sleep. But the second bowl ends up at his door. For the first time she wants to do something for him that isn't a deal.

cliffhanger.text: She sets the bowl on the floor by the door, fork across the rim, and walks away. Behind the door, a chair creaks.
cliffhanger.question: Will he eat it?

spectacle: The concrete hallway is dark except for a line of light under the study door; on the floor, a bowl of pasta still steaming.
glamour_shot: Under the warm kitchen light, low ponytail, she plates the pasta; steam blurs her profile, and there's an ease at the corner of her mouth she hasn't noticed.
general_payoffs: For the first time she does something for him unasked
locations: The Ashford house on the hill (kitchen, living room, outside the study)

title: Salty.
youtube_title: The bowl she left at his door came back with a one-word note
logline: The bowl comes back washed with a note under it. Nora laughs for the first time since she moved in. The same day, Grant goes on TV.
hook: Morning. The bowl sits on the counter, washed spotless. Under it, a sticky note with one word: "Salty."
mid_hook: She reads it and laughs out loud, the first time since she moved in. On the stairs, Theo types fast: "Mrs. Ashford Observation Log. Day 40. She laughed."
extra_hooks: Peg snatches the note and glares at the study. "Too salty? He cleaned the bowl."
conflict: She wants to know what the man behind that door thinks. He answers with one word, and it says more than every clause he's ever written.
turn: She expects the bowl back untouched, or never touched at all. Instead it's eaten, washed, and critiqued. He answered her in his own way.

cliffhanger.text: On the living-room TV, Grant sits on a business-show couch in a pale suit, leaning in. "My ex-wife? Divorced at noon, married to a billionaire by five." The host: "Where is she now?" He smiles. "Kiln Row."
cliffhanger.question: He gave out her street. Now?

spectacle: Morning light on the counter: a gleaming white bowl pinning a small yellow sticky note, the sun landing right on the word.
glamour_shot: She laughs with the note in her hand, pushing her hair back; morning light catches her crinkled eyes, like glass letting light through for the first time.
general_payoffs: The pasta is gone; under the bowl, one word: "Salty."
She laughs for the first time since moving in
Theo's log: Day 40. She laughed.
locations: The Ashford house on the hill (kitchen, living room)

title: Nobody Swings
youtube_title: Press at her door. She grabbed his wrist: "Nobody swings."
logline: One word from Grant, and by dawn the press has Remelt surrounded. Nora has to keep the furnace going, keep Sparks inside, and keep to the front-door rule. Then the ferry terminal calls.
hook: Dawn. Kiln Row is packed with cameras, fists banging Remelt's steel door. Lyle Becker's lens is jammed in the gap: "Ms. Quinn! How's it feel to marry a billionaire?"
mid_hook: Sparks grabs a blowpipe and heads for the door. She clamps his wrist. "Nobody swings. They film you once, we lose."
extra_hooks: Over the shutter clicks her phone rings. Fiona Marsh: "Entry 09. The terminal wants it." Behind her, Number Three burns red.
conflict: Outside, the reporters Grant sent. Inside, a furnace that can't stop and an apprentice shaking with rage. She can't go out and argue, and nobody can throw a punch.
turn: She thinks she'll spend the day trapped and photographed. Then the blind-review result calls: an unsigned chandelier just answered "she married money."

cliffhanger.text: A clang on the steel door. The woman from the chowder shack on the corner bangs a soup ladle on it, apron still on. "Go shoot your own family!" Every lens swings toward her.
cliffhanger.question: Who is the ladle woman?

spectacle: Dawn on Kiln Row: a row of camera flashes popping outside Remelt's steel door, the orange glow of Furnace No. 3 leaking through the gap.
glamour_shot: She stands inside the steel door gripping Sparks's wrist, shoulder-length hair, work apron; flashes strobe across her face through the gap and she doesn't blink.
general_payoffs: Remelt wins the ferry terminal chandelier blind review: her first commission since the divorce
Sparks stays inside and gives the press nothing

title: You've Gotten Thin
youtube_title: She ran off the press, sat her down: "You've gotten thin."
logline: Rosa clears the street of reporters single-handed, then drags Nora in for chowder. She looks at Nora a beat too long, says nothing, and lets slip one line no stranger would say.
hook: Rosa plants herself, ladle up, grey crop, old silver bangle. "Get my sign in the shot. Free advertising!" One by one the cameras drop and back off.
mid_hook: She pulls Nora into the shack and sets down a bowl with a thunk. "Eat." At the stove she looks at Nora a beat too long. Says nothing.
extra_hooks: Sparks slurps chowder in the doorway. "Extra crackers?" Rosa doesn't turn around. "Get 'em yourself."
conflict: Nora wants to thank this stranger and find out why she helped. Rosa will give her chowder and not one answer.
turn: Nora thinks Rosa just hates reporters. But that look isn't for a stranger. It's someone checking a face she saw a long time ago.

cliffhanger.text: Nora finishes and stands to thank her. Rosa, back turned, stirs the pot. "You've gotten thin." Nora stops at the door. "Have we met?" Rosa doesn't turn. "Finish your bowl first."
cliffhanger.question: How does Rosa know her?

spectacle: Steam from the big pot at Rosa's rolls out the door and down Kiln Row, blurring the retreating reporters and their cameras.
glamour_shot: She eats in the shack's steam, hair tucked behind her ear; the heat brings some color back to her pale face, and her eyes finally ease.
general_payoffs: The press is gone and Remelt's door is clear
Her first hot meal cooked by someone else since she left the Glass House
locations: Rosa's, the chowder shack on the corner of Kiln Row

title: The First Marriage Certificate
youtube_title: The best old signature? Her marriage certificate with her ex
logline: Wexler needs a pre-marriage signature held by someone else. Dana finds it: the marriage certificate Nora and Grant signed six years ago at the County Clerk, with another name on the witness line.
hook: Dana slaps the court's return on the light box. "Signatures held by someone else? Two. Your bank signature card at eighteen. And your marriage certificate with him."
mid_hook: On the County Clerk's copy, her signature at twenty-five sits next to Grant's, the last stroke flicking out. Next to the traced ones on the light box, the difference is obvious.
extra_hooks: The chandelier's third blue panel comes out of the annealer. Sparks holds it up. "This one's straight!" She glances. "Rim's off a quarter inch." Sparks: "...Crooked. Twenty-four."
conflict: Fisk says her own drafts don't count. She needs a signature she can't touch or alter, locked in someone else's cabinet for six years.
turn: She thinks the hard part is finding a sample. What turns up is the last paper she wants to see: her marriage certificate with Grant. The day he married her, he filed the best evidence against himself.

cliffhanger.text: On the certificate's witness line: "Margaret Whitlock." Peg stares at her own name from six years ago and takes off her glasses. "Back then I didn't like you." Her hand finds the ledger's cover, stops, and lets go.
cliffhanger.question: What's hidden in Peg's ledger?

spectacle: Three papers side by side on the light box: the six-year-old marriage certificate, the bank card from age eighteen, the traced agreement. The same name three times; only one pauses at every stroke.
glamour_shot: She holds the certificate copy to the light box; light through the paper lights her eyes as she looks at her twenty-five-year-old signature, face perfectly still.
general_payoffs: The court obtains two pre-marriage signatures held by others: the bank signature card and the six-year-old marriage certificate
The chandelier reaches its third panel

title: Mom, It's Salty
youtube_title: Her husband walked into Rosa's: "Mom, it's salty."
logline: Nora brings Rosa a crooked cup Sparks blew and learns Rosa is Elias's mother. That same night, Fisk moves to throw out the whole examination.
hook: Night. She sets a small blue cup on the counter at Rosa's. "Sparks made it. It's crooked." Rosa holds it to the light. "Good. Nobody'll mix it up."
mid_hook: The door chime rings. Elias walks in, black turtleneck, left hand in his pocket, and takes the stool by the counter like he owns it. Rosa: "Eaten?" He tastes the chowder. "Mom. It's salty." Nora's spoon stops in midair.
extra_hooks: Outside she asks, "She's your mother?" "Yes." "Why does she run a chowder shack on Kiln Row?" He looks down the dark old street. "She likes this street."
conflict: She came to thank the woman who chased off the reporters. That woman is Elias's mother, and Elias never said a word.
turn: She thinks Rosa is a kind neighbor. One word, "Mom," flips it: "You've gotten thin" and the "Salty." under the bowl came from the same family.

cliffhanger.text: In the car home, Dana calls. "Fisk moved to replace the examiner. Says he went to your studio, so he's biased. If it's granted, we start over."
cliffhanger.question: Will the report get blocked?

spectacle: Night on Kiln Row, only Rosa's lit; steam from the big pot drifts out the door, and three people stand in it, none of them speaking first.
glamour_shot: Elias on the stool at Rosa's, head down over the chowder, black turtleneck, thin-framed glasses fogged; when he looks up and says "It's salty," for once he looks like someone's son.
general_payoffs: She learns Rosa is Elias's mother
"Salty" is his word: he wrote the note under the bowl himself
locations: Rosa's, the chowder shack on the corner of Kiln Row

title: Likely Done Left-Handed
youtube_title: Traced. Dated her night in the hospital. Done left-handed.
logline: The court denies Fisk's motion and the report arrives: the signatures are traced, and the agreement is dated the night she was under anesthesia. The forgery charge is filed, and the report's last line points to a left hand.
hook: The ruling comes first: "Samples were taken under court order with both counsel present. Motion denied." Dana sets it down. "Report's here this afternoon."
mid_hook: The report: both signatures, on the agreement and the rights transfer, are traced, not hers. The agreement's date matches Merrow General's anesthesia record: the night she lay in the hospital, knowing nothing.
extra_hooks: The court freezes the transfers of the Glass House and the accounts. A letter from the prosecutor: forgery charge filed. She walks to the wall and pushes the bead from Report to Charges. Ding. Peg's pen stops.
conflict: Fisk wants the examination thrown out and redone; Grant wants time. All she wants is a report in black and white that shows the judge what she sees.
turn: She expects the report to say the signatures are fake. It also matches the date: the agreement that "gave him everything" was signed the night she was under anesthesia, when she couldn't open her eyes.

cliffhanger.text: She turns to the report's last line: "The tracing was likely done left-handed." A flash: Sienna on the launch stage, turning her notes with her left hand. And the day at the Glass House, Sienna signing the curtain delivery slip, left-handed. Nora, quietly: "Left."
cliffhanger.question: Whose left hand traced her?

spectacle: In the glass tube on the brick wall, a bead slides from Report to Charges and stops with a ding; beside it the twelve empty slots of the evidence rack shine in the furnace light.
glamour_shot: She reads the report's last line at the light box, lit from below, hair falling onto the page; when she lifts her eyes they're cold as glass fresh from the annealer.
general_payoffs: The signature on the property agreement is exposed: traced from her pre-marriage drafts, pausing at every stroke and missing the final flick; dated the night she was under anesthesia at Merrow General; the Forever rights transfer was traced by the same hand
The court freezes the transfers of the Glass House and the accounts
The forgery charge is filed; the bead moves to Charges
